claims.claim: **A foreskin that won't retract is a normal variant needing no intervention** — it is not true phimosis. Full retraction is possible in 10% by 1 year, 50% by 10 years and 99% by 17 years.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Never forcibly retract the foreskin for cleaning.** Once it retracts naturally, retract it in the bath and **replace it immediately** to prevent paraphimosis.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Smegma lumps and residual foreskin attachments are normal** and need no intervention; smegma discharge is sometimes mistaken for pus.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Problematic ballooning:** betamethasone 0.05% sparingly to the preputial ring three times daily for 6–12 weeks (success over 90%, recurrence up to 17%). **Only pathological phimosis makes circumcision indicated.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Minor redness or soreness at the foreskin tip:** reassurance and avoiding chemical and physical triggers.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Balanitis:** warm weak salt-water soaks; barrier cream or 1% hydrocortisone; clotrimazole or miconazole if candida is suspected; oral analgesia as needed.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Topical antibiotics are not effective or recommended**, and **do not retract the foreskin during acute inflammation** — it can cause paraphimosis.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Secondary bacterial infection or cellulitis:** cefalexin 20 mg/kg (max 750 mg) orally three times daily for 7 days. **Send urine culture if febrile** to exclude UTI.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Group A streptococcus can cause a severe weeping, raw genital rash.** Swabs are not routinely recommended as they are often contaminated — treat on clinical merit.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pathological phimosis = scarring of the preputial ring**: a visible scar ring, non-retractable at the end of puberty, a previously retractable foreskin that no longer retracts, or persistent ballooning with a pinhole opening unresponsive to steroid.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Trial betamethasone 0.05% cream 2–3 times daily for 2–4 weeks**; if it works, continue to a total of 6–12 weeks. **No or poor response → paediatric surgery.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Urgent surgical referral if the child cannot pass urine.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Paraphimosis is a urological emergency** with risk of preputial necrosis, but can usually be corrected without surgery.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Oral analgesia, then a firm compression bandage (ideally 1 inch) from the penile tip over the oedema for 10–15 minutes**, then attempt reduction; if that fails, re-bandage for a further 15 minutes and retry.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Failed manual reduction → urgent surgical consult. Dusky or dark tissue → urgent paediatric surgeon review.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **After reduction, no circumcision or follow-up is needed.** Advise no retraction for a few days, retract only for cleaning, and always replace fully.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Zipper entrapment:** oral analgesia ± sedation; cut the median bar of the slider, then across the zipper, with wire cutters, and separate the teeth. **Glans injury → paediatric surgery.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Hair tourniquet in infants:** red, swollen distal penis with a demarcation line — **divide the fibre or hair ring** and check skin integrity; ask a senior if unsure.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Medical indications for circumcision: pathological phimosis or recurrent UTIs.** An inflamed, crusted glans afterwards is common; petroleum jelly to the nappy or a liner for a few days may help.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Significant post-circumcision bleeding:** apply compression, get urgent surgical advice and **consider coagulopathy.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Priapism (erection over 4 hours) is a surgical emergency**; commonest causes: sickle cell disease 65% · trauma 10% · leukaemia 10%.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Older children:** urination, running up stairs, a cold bath or cold packs — ⚠️ **no cold packs if the child could have sickle cell disease.** Seek care early if not resolved in under 2 hours.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consult the paediatric or surgical team for:** inability to pass urine · paraphimosis with ischaemia · priapism · zipper injury involving the glans.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23
